entries.name: Market square
entries.purpose: civic and commercial heart of a town: weekly market, fairs, proclamations, occasional executions
parts: open paved space
well or fountain at the centre
market cross
town hall on one side
rows of market stalls on market days
layout: rectangular or triangular open space where streets converge
stalls set in rows, often aligned with the cross
facades fronted with shops and inns on the ground floor
entries.found: in virtually every old market town of Europe and its colonial diaspora
entries.notes: A market charter was the economic engine of a medieval town: holding a licensed market, fair day and toll was often its main source of municipal revenue. Look for the market cross as the legal anchor of the space.

entries.name: Souk / suq (Arab market street)
entries.purpose: permanent market streets, organized strictly by trade, serving the medina
parts: vaulted or canopied alley
cell-like shops one bay wide
caravanserai lodging at the rear of the block
guild sections: spices, textiles, metals, leather
layout: narrow lanes, one or two carts wide
trades grouped together: goldsmiths at one end, grain at the other
covered where sun and rain demand it, open where they do not
entries.found: throughout the medinas of the Arab and Turkish world — Fez, Marrakech, Damascus, Cairo, Aleppo
entries.notes: Damascus's Souk al-Hamidiyya (opened 1884, roofed like a Roman colonnade with a corrugated iron vault) is a classic example. The trade-by-street rule means spice, silk and copper each have their own lane.

entries.name: Farmers' market
entries.era: 20th century to now (older roots in weekly markets)
entries.purpose: direct sale of farm produce from grower to consumer
parts: rows of farm stalls
produce crates and scales
piknik tables or coffee under a tree
sometimes a band or buskers
layout: weekly or twice-weekly, morning to midday
stalls in loose rows on a town square, car park or street
growers often sell from the back of a pickup or van
entries.found: every town of reasonable size in Europe and North America, often Saturday mornings
entries.notes: Pike Place Market (Seattle, 1907) is the canonical modern example, opened to let farmers bypass wholesalers. Certified farmers' markets ban reselling and guarantee producer-only stalls.

entries.name: Piazza (Italian public square)
entries.purpose: outdoor room of the Italian city: market by day, promenade and politics by night
parts: open paved space
central fountain or equestrian statue
arcaded logge (colonnades)
church and campanile on one side
layout: enclosed by continuous facades, often arcaded at ground level
cafe tables ringing the periphery
one monumental axis, usually toward the church facade
entries.found: every Italian town and city; Piazza San Marco (Venice), Piazza della Signoria (Florence), Piazza del Campo (Siena)
entries.notes: Piazza San Marco is about 175 x 80 m and was called 'the drawing room of Europe' by Napoleon. Italian piazzas double as market squares in the morning and passeggiata stage at dusk.

entries.name: Plaza mayor / plaza de armas (enclosed Spanish market square)
entries.purpose: enclosed ceremonial market and civic square of Spain and Spanish America
parts: uniform arcaded buildings on all four sides
iron or timber balconies above the portales
equestrian statue (Madrid: Philip III)
one or two monumental entrances (Madrid: Arco de Cuchilleros)
layout: strictly rectangular, enclosed on all sides
portales (arcades) at street level, balconies above
in Latin America the plaza de armas sits at the crossing of the main street, usually with a bandstand
entries.found: Madrid, Seville, Cusco, Quito, Lima, Mexico City — anywhere the Spanish city grid placed its main square
entries.notes: Madrid's Plaza Mayor (completed 1619 by Juan Gómez de Mora) measures 129 x 94 m with 237 balconies; bullfights, autos-da-fé and markets all filled this one space.

entries.name: Agora (Greek public square)
entries.era: archaic to late antiquity (c. 800 BCE to c. 500 CE)
entries.purpose: assembly, marketplace, law courts and religious centre of the Greek polis
parts: stoas (covered colonnades with shops) on one or more sides
bouleuterion (council house)
altar of the Twelve Gods (Athens)
law courts and statues of civic heroes
layout: open rectangle ringed by civic buildings and stoas
sacred altar or altar of the gods at one edge
markets on the stoas' ground floor, courts behind
entries.found: every Greek city; the Athenian Agora is the best preserved
entries.notes: 'Agora' meant both the gathering and the place. In 5th-century BCE Athens it was the one space where common citizens could watch ostracisms, trials and market trade in a single glance.

entries.name: Grand Place / Grote Markt (guildhall square)
materials: stone and brick guildhouses with gilded facades
entries.purpose: guild and mercantile showpiece of the Low Countries: markets, fairs and civic ceremony
parts: opulent guildhouses on the long sides
town hall (belfry up to ~96 m)
Maison du Roi / Bread house
open cobbled centre
layout: rectangular open space enclosed by one storey of ornate gabled facades
brewers', bakers' and weavers' guildhouses compete in height and gold leaf
carillon tower dominating the skyline
entries.found: Brussels, Antwerp, Bruges, Ghent and the other great cloth towns of the Low Countries
entries.notes: Brussels' Grand Place was bombarded by French troops in 1695; the guilds rebuilt in stone, grander and gilded, earning it UNESCO status in 1998. The Bread House opposite the town hall began as the city's bread market.

entries.name: Red Square (Moscow)
entries.purpose: parade ground, market and political stage of Russia
parts: Lobnoye Mesto herald's platform
St Basil's Cathedral at the south end
Lenin's Mausoleum against the Kremlin wall
GUM department store arcade on the east side
State Historical Museum at the north end
layout: longitudinal axis along the Kremlin wall
open centre used for military parades and public festivals
monumental buildings on three sides, open to the Moskva River view
entries.found: Moscow, Russia
entries.notes: The name originally meant 'beautiful square' or the 'burnt-out place' after fires cleared the site. It hosted markets, then coronations, executions, revolutions and May Day parades in turn.

entries.name: Tiananmen Square (Beijing)
entries.purpose: nationalist ceremonial square on Beijing's central axis
parts: Tiananmen (Gate of Heavenly Peace) on the north side
Mao Zedong Mausoleum at the south
Great Hall of the People on the west
National Museum on the east
Monument to the People's Heroes (38 m) in the centre
layout: north-south ceremonial axis, 880 x 500 m (~440,000 m2)
symmetric massing around the Monument to the People's Heroes
flag-raising ceremony each morning at dawn
entries.found: Beijing, China
entries.notes: Created in 1651 outside the imperial palace gate, quadrupled in the 1950s by demolition of surrounding old office quarters. Famous for the 1949 founding proclamation and for the 1989 protests and crackdown.

entries.name: Times Square (New York)
entries.purpose: commercial and entertainment crossroads of Midtown Manhattan
parts: bow-tie crossing of Broadway and Seventh Avenue (42nd-47th Streets)
tiered LED billboards
Broadway theatres facing the square
the New Year's Eve ball
layout: two intersecting avenues create a wedge-shaped pedestrian zone
facades layered with illuminated signage
dense pedestrian flow day and night — over 300,000 people daily
entries.found: New York City, USA
entries.notes: Named for The New York Times, whose headquarters opened here in 1904. The New Year's Eve ball drop on One Times Square has run since 1907 and draws over a million live viewers annually.

entries.name: Market cross
entries.purpose: the legal and ceremonial anchor of a market charter: tolls, proclamations, punishments
parts: stepped base (3-8 steps)
carved shaft, sometimes with canopy or small chapel
cross wheel or simple iron cross at the top
layout: placed at the centre of the market place
usually aligned to the town hall or church
in some towns (Salisbury, Chichester) it shelters an open chapel under the canopy
entries.found: market towns across England, Ireland, France, Spain (crucero) and the Low Countries
entries.notes: Market crosses are not religious objects primarily: they marked where the king's proclamation was read and where market tolls were enforced. Many were 'restored' in the 19th century; few survive untouched.

entries.name: Night market
entries.purpose: evening open-air food and goods market for the after-work crowd
parts: rows of identical food stalls (noodles, dumplings, skewers, desserts)
retail stalls at the far end
funfair games in some
plastic stools for dining on the spot
layout: long street or alley closed to traffic at dusk
stall rows on both sides with a central walkway
works best where the daytime is too hot or too busy for shopping
entries.found: every major Taiwanese city (Shilin, Raohe), Hong Kong, Taipei, Bangkok, Hanoi, Manila
entries.notes: Taiwan's night markets are the world benchmark — Shilin's stretch is ~300 m of stalls under one roof of signs. They exist where daytime office and factory hours push all retail life into the evening.

entries.name: Fish market
entries.purpose: landing, grading, auction and first sale of the catch before it enters a city
parts: auction floor with sloped concrete
ice storage and delivery bays
grading tables and scales
cold room for premium tuna
retail stalls at the public edge
layout: close to the dock or landing pier
dawn auctions before dawn, retail by morning
ice flows in a heavy layer, scrubbed off at night
entries.found: every serious fishing port; Tokyo (Tsukiji until 2018, now Toyosu), Sydney (Pyrmont), Seattle (Pike Place Market, retail since 1907)
entries.notes: Tsukiji was the world's largest fish and seafood market by volume; its inner wholesale market moved to Toyosu in October 2018, leaving the outer retail market in place.

entries.name: Mandi (Indian regulated wholesale produce market)
entries.purpose: regulated wholesale sale of fruit and vegetables under APMC law
parts: auction floors with raised podiums for the auctioneer
chilled stores and grading rooms
weighbridge at the gate
commission agents' (arhatiya) offices
layout: huge dusty or concreted yards at the edge of the city or nearest railhead
trucks tip produce at one end, buyers sort it at the other
trading runs 3-6 am to noon, sleepy after 2 pm
entries.found: every Indian mandi town; Azadpur (Delhi) handles ~8,000-10,000 tonnes a day
entries.notes: Azadpur is cited as Asia's largest fruit and vegetable wholesale market (~100 acres). Mandis fix the farm-gate price for half a billion growers; reform of the APMC Acts is a running political battle.

entries.name: Mercado (covered municipal market)
entries.purpose: municipal covered retail market for fresh food and household goods
parts: iron-and-glass central hall
individual stall counters in trade sections
butchery and fishmonger rows with tiled floor drains
food counters at the rear
layout: rectangular hall with a central nave and side aisles
fish and meat at one end, produce and flowers at the other
some stalls lease to third generations with the same trade
entries.found: every large Iberian and Latin American city — Mercado de la Merced (Mexico City), Mercado Central (Santiago), Mercat de la Boqueria (Barcelona)
entries.notes: The form arrived with 19th-century iron engineering and municipal sanitation drives. Many are now tourist icons (Boqueria) or redevelopment battlegrounds (La Merced).

entries.name: Tianguis (Mexican street market)
entries.purpose: weekly or daily open-air market strung along a closed street
parts: stall lanes: produce, hardware, clothing, toys, food
marchantes' wheeled carts between rows
roving tortilla sellers with baskets on their heads
layout: one closed street or a network of streets at the market day
rows of stalls back to back, single-file lanes for buyers
assembles in under an hour, gone by evening
entries.found: every Mexican city; the word descends from Nahuatl tianquiztli
entries.notes: Tlatelolco's market stunned Cortes's chroniclers — so dense it was impossible to see across. Today tianguis days empty supermarkets and form the main retail lifeline of working-class colonias.

entries.name: Wet market
entries.purpose: daily retail of fresh meat, fish and produce — food bought fresh every day
parts: sloped floor with central drain
cold tables and ice boxes for meat and fish
live tanks or hanging poultry at some stalls
open produce baskets on the floor or on low shelves
layout: open-air or open-fronted, often just a roof and drains
sellers rinse everything constantly — that is the 'wet'
sections by product, always noisy and crowded at dawn
entries.found: every Chinese and Southeast Asian city, and most Korean and Taiwanese neighbourhoods
entries.notes: 'Wet' refers only to the floor kept flushed with water. Wet markets remain where households cook with fresh ingredients daily; they are being slowly squeezed by supermarkets and hygiene rules.

entries.name: Shotengai (Japanese covered shopping arcade)
entries.purpose: covered shopping street of independent shops for daily goods and food
parts: arcade roof over the full street width
continuous small shops 4-8 m frontage
arcade tannoy and clock at the centre
entrance arches with market name
layout: single or multi-block straight covered street
one-way pedestrian with arcaded stalls either side
arcades often follow the old road line under the modern roof
entries.found: throughout Japan — over 800 shotengai across the country, e.g. Kyoto's Teramachi and Osaka's covered arcades
entries.notes: Shotengai were the working-class retail backbone after the 1923 Kanto earthquake; many now struggle against malls, but basement and side-street arcades still feed daily life.

entries.name: Sijang (Korean traditional market)
entries.purpose: oldest living market tradition of Korea: food, fabric, street cooking
parts: covered food rows (mayak kimbap, bindaetteok, yukhoe)
fabric and hanbok sellers' row
raw-material (oil, grain) stalls
eating alleys with shared tables
layout: dense covered block between two streets
cooking stalls at the entrance edge to draw in passers-by
cash and haggling; plastic stools and metal chopsticks
entries.found: Seoul (Gwangjang, est. 1905), plus Namdaemun, Dongdaemun and every provincial city
entries.notes: Gwangjang opened 1905 as Korea's first permanent daily market; it covers ~42,000 m2 with 5,000+ shops and ~65,000 daily visitors, famous for mung-bean pancakes and raw-beef tartare.

entries.name: Chợ (Vietnamese market)
entries.purpose: central municipal market of a Vietnamese city
parts: four gates (Ben Thanh: S, N, E, W), clock tower on the south
interior stall grid by trade
produce hall and dried goods
souvenir and textile alleys for tourists
layout: large single-storey hall with high arched roof
street stalls and food carts sprawl outside the gates after dark
produce in the sheds, souvenirs and tourists at the front rows
entries.found: every Vietnamese city; Ben Thanh Market (Ho Chi Minh City, 1912-1914) is the famous one
entries.notes: Ben Thanh's three-faced clock tower on Le Loi street is the postcard of Saigon. The 13,056 m2 hall holds ~1,500 stalls and some 3,000 vendors; renovation in 2022 kept the 1914 shell.

entries.name: Livestock market
entries.purpose: sale and auction of cattle, sheep and horses before slaughter or breeding
parts: open holding pens and crush lanes
central auction ring with raised podium
drovers' lodging and hay barns
weighbridge
layout: large yards on the edge of town or beside a railway
long pens feeding into a central ring
sale days weekly, dawn to midday
entries.found: market towns across Europe and North America; Smithfield (London) ran livestock from at least the 12th century
entries.notes: Smithfield's live cattle trade ended in 1855 (moved to Islington); Horace Jones's 1868 Central Market roof converted it to wholesale meat, the iron-and-glass hall that still stands.

entries.name: Flea market
entries.purpose: resale of second-hand goods, antiques and salvage
parts: eleven or so specialist markets in one
antiques, rag-and-bone booths, food stalls
salvage rows of furniture and architectural scrap
layout: labyrinth of open-air aisles on the city fringe
dealers arrive before dawn on weekends
haggling is the point, not a failure of retail
entries.found: Paris (Marché aux Puces de Saint-Ouen, 1870s), London (Portobello Road, 1948), Berlin (Boxhagener Platz), every big city
entries.notes: The Marché aux Puces de Saint-Ouen covers about 7 hectares with several thousand stalls — the largest antiques market in the world. 'Puces' (fleas) comes from the rag-and-bone sellers of the 19th century.

entries.name: Cloth hall
entries.purpose: wholesale hall where the cloth guild sold and measured cloth by the bolt
parts: long single or two-bay trading hall
stall divisions down the centre
attic storey with civic or guild rooms above
sometimes a belfry or watch tower
layout: a single long hall in the exact centre of the market square
roofline lower than town hall, higher than shops
colonnade or arcade at the ground floor for measuring cloth
entries.found: Kraków (Sukiennice, Renaissance 1557), Bruges (late medieval), Ypres (1304, rebuilt), Chester and Shrewsbury in England
entries.notes: The Flemish cloth towns made Europe's medieval fortune, and their great halls expressed that wealth. Ypres's Cloth Hall (1304) is one of the largest medieval civic buildings north of the Alps.

entries.name: Waag (weigh house)
entries.purpose: public weighing of bulk goods (cheese, grain, cloth, meat) for toll and customs
parts: large balance beam across the ground floor
sets of beam scales for different goods
toll and seal rooms above
often an upper council room or small museum
layout: open ground floor usable for goods wagons to drive through
tower or gable over the entrance with the town's coat of arms
central spot near the market hall or harbour
entries.found: the Low Countries and northern Germany; Amsterdam's Waag (1488, built as St Anthony's Gate), Haarlem, Delft, Hoorn
entries.notes: The waag was where every barrel, bale and side of bacon was officially weighed before duty; its surviving scales are among the largest accurate balances ever built by hand.

entries.name: Corn exchange
entries.purpose: wholesale trading floor where grain prices were fixed for a district
parts: circular or oval central trading floor
cast-iron gallery ring
domed glazed roof
weigh rooms and committee rooms below
layout: round or elliptical plan for maximum sight-lines across the trading floor
dome lights the centre; ring of balcony for brokers
entrances aligned to the market square
entries.found: agricultural market towns of Britain and Ireland; Leeds Corn Exchange (1863, Cuthbert Brodrick) is the masterpiece
entries.notes: Leeds's oval, glass-domed hall is 160 x 136 ft (~49 x 41 m) and ~75 ft (23 m) to the inner dome. After the Corn Laws were repealed in 1846 and the railway killed the grain fair, most became theatres and shopping arcades.

entries.name: Les Halles (Paris central wholesale market)
entries.era: market on site since 1131; Baltard pavilions 1854-1973
entries.purpose: the wholesale stomach of Paris — fresh food distribution for the whole city
parts: ten cast-iron and glass pavilions (Baltard)
vast sprung roofs with no interior columns
surrounding narrow market streets for butchers, grocers, fishmongers
fountain at the centre
layout: compact rectangular block in the heart of Paris
nightly truck unloading from midnight
morning wholesale until dawn, then sweep and reset for the next day
entries.found: central Paris, demolished 1973 (today the Forum des Halles)
entries.notes: Zola called them 'the belly of Paris'; Baltard's pavilions were so daringly light that passersby feared they would blow away. One pavilion survives at Nogent-sur-Marne; the rest went to the scrapyard in 1973.

entries.name: Royal Exchange (London)
materials: cast iron and glass courtyard roof
entries.purpose: merchant's meeting house and courtyard exchange for commodities and later finance
parts: open courtyard arcade for merchants to walk and trade
Corinthian portico on Threadneedle Street
upper-floor shops and offices
statue of Gresham in the courtyard
layout: rectangular block around an open courtyard
no trading floor — deals struck while walking the arcade
adjacent to the Bank of England and Lloyd's Coffee House
entries.found: Threadneedle Street, London
entries.notes: Thomas Gresham opened it in 1571 as a meeting place for merchants of every nation; it was London's commercial cockpit for 300 years. Burned in the Great Fire (1666), rebuilt 1669; current facade is William Tite's 1844 replacement.

entries.name: Amsterdam Beurs (first stock exchange building)
entries.purpose: commodities and securities exchange — the template of every modern stock market
parts: open courtyard for walking trade
arcades with named posts for each commodity (VOC, WIC, spices, grain, timber)
bell to open and close the trading day
layout: rectangular block over the Rokin watercourse on Dam Square
continuous arcade on three sides for VOC shares and commodities
merchants met under the arches, never inside a hall
entries.found: Rokin, Amsterdam (the de Keyser building was replaced in 1835)
entries.notes: VOC (Dutch East India Company, 1602) issued the world's first tradable shares; de Keyser's 1611 Beurs on the Rokin housed the secondary market. The institution lives on as Euronext Amsterdam.

entries.name: Stoa of Attalos (reconstructed)
entries.purpose: two-storey covered market row of shops facing the Athenian Agora
parts: 21 shops on each of two floors
Doric exterior colonnade below, Ionic above
rear walls with doorways to storage and upper floors
layout: single long slab along the east side of the Agora
open colonnade facing the square, shops behind
upper floor reached by internal stairs at each end
entries.found: Athens, Greece (east edge of the Agora)
entries.notes: A gift of Attalus II of Pergamon to Athens. Meticulously rebuilt by the American School of Classical Studies (1952-56) using the original foundations and materials — now the Agora Museum.

entries.name: Macellum (Roman covered meat and fish market)
entries.purpose: covered hall for the retail of meat, fish and oysters
parts: open courtyard with central tholos (round fountain kiosk)
ring of tabernae (shops) on all four sides
shaded colonnades for weighing and haggling
fish scales and hooks mounted on the walls
layout: rectangular courtyard building in the city centre, near the forum
tholos in the middle for a sacred spring or deity (often Mercury)
fish kept on ice from the mountains, meat hung indoors
entries.found: every Roman city; best preserved at Pompeii and Lepcis Magna
entries.notes: The word survives in Italian macelleria and French macellerie. Nero's Macellum Magnum (59 CE, Rome, Caelian Hill) was the monumental imperial version, with two storeyed arcades.

entries.name: Qaysariyya (Persian covered luxury trade hall)
entries.purpose: lockable, high-value core of the bazaar: silk, carpets, jewellery, spice
parts: tall vaulted hall with a domed central crossing
cell-like shops with sturdy iron-bound doors
upper storage and office floors
ceremonial gateway (pishtaq) to the street
layout: the most guarded block inside the bazaar, often near the Friday mosque
domed crossings light the centre; vaults run in all directions
gates locked at night, opened by the bazaar elders
entries.found: Isfahan (Qeysariyeh gate, 1602, Abbas I), Shiraz, Tabriz, Yazd and other Safavid-era trade cities
entries.notes: The Qeysariyeh gate of Isfahan still marks the entrance to the Grand Bazaar — its portal was once topped with metal statues of mythical beasts. Qaysariyya sold only the bazaar's most valuable goods.

entries.name: Jemaa el-Fnaa (Marrakech)
entries.purpose: public square of storytellers, musicians, healers and food stalls — a civic theatre
parts: halqa rings of spectators around storytellers and acrobats
orange-juice carts with mounds of fruit
evening grill stalls (hundreds of sheep and chickens)
traditional healers and tooth-pullers at the edges
layout: huge open rectangle south-west of the Koutoubia mosque minaret
performers form by mid-morning, gone by late evening
tight alleys of the souk radiate from the square's north-east corner
entries.found: Marrakech medina, Morocco
entries.notes: UNESCO Intangible Cultural Heritage (proclaimed 2001, inscribed 2008). The name may mean 'assembly of the dead', recalling public executions staged here; today it is the largest open-air food court in North Africa.

entries.name: Floating market (talat nam)
entries.purpose: canal-based market where boats are the shops, sellers and sometimes the shoppers
parts: sampan boats loaded with produce, cooked food or souvenirs
long-tail boats ferrying shoppers between boats
canal-side piers with stalls and kitchens
layout: long canal reach that narrows so boats queue single-file
sellers announce wares by boat, buyers flag them down from the bank
early morning peak before 9 am, heat and quiet by noon
entries.found: Bangkok canals and Damnoen Saduak (dug 1866 under King Mongkut Rama IV), Amphawa
entries.notes: Damnoen Saduak has been tourism-first for decades; real Bangkok fresh-food trade long since moved to wholesale markets. Even so, a canal full of loaded sampans at dawn is still the working image of old Siam.

entries.name: Tang-dynasty market wards (fang shih)
entries.purpose: walled, gated commercial enclosures of the imperial capital — officially the only legal place to trade
parts: perimeter wall with eight gates
cross streets dividing the ward into nine blocks
thousands of shops in trade-specific rows
government tax offices and a bell tower at the centre
layout: Eastern and Western Markets of Chang'an, each ~1,025 x 925 m
gates opened on the morning drum, closed at the evening bell
foreign merchants (Persian, Sogdian, Arab) clustered in the West Market
entries.found: Chang'an (Xi'an), Tang capital and the largest city on Earth c. 750
entries.notes: Each market had eight gates, four main streets and a strict opening schedule. By the late Tang, enforcing the gates failed and night trading spilled into the wards — the birth of the night market.

entries.name: Haat (weekly rural market)
entries.purpose: periodic rural market: one day a week, the entire village economy in one place
parts: rows of bamboo stalls by trade
livestock pen at one end
food and tea stalls with clay cups
moneylender and weighing scale corners
layout: open field or wide road junction used only on market day
arrive by bullock cart before dawn, gone by noon
buyers walk from every village within a half-day's walk
entries.found: eastern and central India and Bangladesh — every rural block
entries.notes: A haat is the oldest retail unit in South Asia: for most villages it was the only access to salt, iron, cloth and news. The English word 'bazaar' reached India via Persian, but the haat was already there.

entries.name: Addis Mercato (Addis Ababa)
entries.purpose: continental wholesale and retail hub: coffee, grain, textiles, scrap, everything
parts: coffee-washing and bagging yards
grain (teff) depots
scrap-metal and electronics rows
wood, furniture and leather sections
layout: vast sprawl over several square km of Addis Ketema district
no single entrance, no map, no centre
wholesale in the morning, retail all day
entries.found: Addis Ababa, Ethiopia
entries.notes: The largest open-air market in Africa — roughly 500 acres with an estimated 13,000 businesses and over 7,000-10,000 stalls and shops. Named under Italian occupation (1936) but an old Ethiopian market long before that.

entries.name: Kejetia market (Kumasi)
entries.purpose: wholesale and retail engine of the Ashanti trade network and of Ghana's north-south trade
parts: open sheds for most stalls
textiles (kente, wax print) rows
foodstuffs and smoked fish sections
electronics and hardware wings
layout: huge central block next to the Kumasi railway station and central bus station
stalls overflow into surrounding streets
multi-storey 2018 redevelopment added hundreds of modern shops
entries.found: Kumasi, Ghana
entries.notes: The largest single open-air market in West Africa — 8,000+ stalls and an estimated 50,000 daily visitors. Kumasi's position made it the trade heart of the old Ashanti Empire and still the junction of Ghana's goods flow.
